cadence: Daily scheduled review; publication follows verified work.

timeline.title: Check the counts behind a blood test
timeline.type: Primary pediatric study and accuracy audit
timeline.summary: One newly indexed study compared blood markers in children with tic disorders and healthy controls. Its accuracy looked high in that small sample, but one reported rate does not match the stated control count. This is not a validated diagnostic test.

timeline.title: What can injury registries tell us?
timeline.type: Historical registry comparison and limited scan
timeline.summary: Two older registry studies tracked serious transport injuries or deaths and traumatic brain injuries. Neither measured whether a tic caused the injury or estimated short-term risk in adults with severe active tics. The limited scan found no qualifying new result.

timeline.title: Which daily activities should a tic assessment ask about?
timeline.type: New pediatric assessment study and limited scan
timeline.summary: A new study asked 19 occupational therapists which daily activities matter when assessing children with tic disorders. Their ratings help identify relevant questions, but do not show whether children’s scores can reliably detect change. No newer trial result or safety warning was verified in the limited scan.

timeline.title: Injury and urgent care are different measures.
timeline.type: Historical measurement comparison and limited scan
timeline.summary: A past clinic study counted emergency visits and hospital stays, while a separate interview counted recently reported behaviors, including some without visible injury. Neither predicts near-term injury. The limited scan found no qualifying new result.

timeline.title: Three different questions about tic-related harm
timeline.type: Historical evidence comparison and limited scan
timeline.summary: A Swedish registry study records long-term neck disorders, while a questionnaire measures recent self-reported burden. Neither estimates near-term injury for adults excluded from an online tic therapy study because they needed urgent care. The limited scan found no qualifying new result.

timeline.title: What zero reported serious events can tell us
timeline.type: Historical safety audit and limited scan
timeline.summary: A small adult online tic therapy pilot reported no serious events, but that does not rule out uncommon harms. Both the pilot and a separate randomized trial exclude tics posing an urgent risk of injury. No new primary result was verified in the limited scan.

timeline.title: Sleep deserves its own measure.
timeline.type: Published model comparison and limited scan
timeline.summary: In two older studies, worse day-to-day impact was linked to worse sleep after narrowing the analysis, but the link was less certain when all factors were included. Sleep still needs its own measure. No new result was verified in the limited scan.

timeline.title: Daily-life measures need their own checks.
timeline.type: Published measurement audit and limited scan
timeline.summary: Three older studies clarified why pain, sleep and participation need separate measures. None established that the scores can be compared across ages and tic severity. No new primary result was verified in the limited scan.

timeline.title: Tic scores and day-to-day impact need separate checks.
timeline.type: Published-study reanalysis and limited scan
timeline.summary: In an older follow-up, none of the reported links passed an exploratory check for multiple comparisons. The study still suggests questions to test in new groups. No new primary result was verified in the limited scan.

timeline.title: A promising measure still needs the right test.
timeline.type: Conference-aggregate audit and access-limited scan
timeline.summary: An adult conference abstract does not yet supply calibrated or treatment-predictive evidence. A reproducible uncertainty check preserves that limit. No new peer-reviewed primary result was verified; registry access was limited.

timeline.title: A new review, and a closer look at what tic measures mean
timeline.type: Secondary evidence and historical comparison
timeline.summary: A new ecopipam review is not a new trial. Three older reports measure different aspects of tics and burden, with shared-cohort and reporting limits. No new primary finding or trial result was verified in the bounded scan; preprint coverage is partial.

timeline.title: Check what a correction changes.
timeline.type: Historical correction audit and limited evidence scan
timeline.summary: The correction text remains unavailable, so its scientific impact is unknown. No existing claim was found to depend on its paper. No new primary tic result was verified; preprint coverage was partial.

timeline.title: A registry date is not a study result.
timeline.type: Evidence scan and analysis-feasibility decision
timeline.summary: One registry moved its estimated start without posting results. No qualifying new primary result was verified. Required analysis inputs remain missing, so closed audits and simulations stayed stopped.

timeline.title: A stopped analysis needs a clear reason.
timeline.type: Evidence scan and analysis-feasibility decision
timeline.summary: No qualifying new clinical evidence was verified. Two registry dates changed without results. Required measurement, map and outcome inputs remain missing; no duplicate analysis or simulation was run.

timeline.title: A measure needs a stable meaning.
timeline.type: Historical measurement-anchor audit and evidence scan
timeline.summary: Six historical reports support useful measurement tools. The inspected evidence does not establish a stable external anchor that separates urge generation from action control. Source-access limits remain; no treatment rule follows.

timeline.title: Precision cannot replace an assumption.
timeline.type: Synthetic measurement methods and evidence scan
timeline.summary: In an artificial model, known stable measurements can distinguish two explanations. An unknown reporting shift makes them indistinguishable; more repeats cannot fix it. No clinical treatment claim follows.

timeline.title: A useful result still has boundaries.
timeline.type: New measurement publication and historical mechanism audit
timeline.summary: A new pediatric video paper has reporting and validation limits. A historical behavioral audit found training signals without a validated personalized treatment rule or durable everyday transfer.

timeline.title: Practiced tics are not the whole picture.
timeline.type: Historical endpoint/protocol audit and evidence scan
timeline.summary: A small youth trial found a trained-tic signal at one week. Untrained-tic and lasting benefit remain unverified; a planned follow-up enrolled nobody. The scan found no qualifying new clinical result.

timeline.title: Check what the background changes.
timeline.type: Historical provenance audit, synthetic methods and evidence scan
timeline.summary: Exact study masks remain unverified. In a synthetic example, adding empty background changes a map score without changing overlap. No clinical result or treatment target follows; the scan found no qualifying new clinical evidence.

timeline.title: Check whether a map can be tested.
timeline.type: Historical group-artifact audit and evidence scan
timeline.summary: Three public group maps passed hash and grid checks. Missing inputs limit replication; no treatment target was validated. The scan found no qualifying new clinical evidence; one registry date changed.

timeline.title: Check what a driving test can show.
timeline.type: Historical aggregate audit and evidence scan
timeline.summary: An adult trial showed a favorable computerized-driving signal. The test hierarchy and unclear denominators limit broad safety claims. The scan found no qualifying new clinical evidence; one registry date changed.

timeline.title: Check the document, not just its label.
timeline.type: Historical trial documentation audit and evidence scan
timeline.summary: An adult trial planned direct function measures. A mislabeled attachment could not resolve missingness questions; no clinical effect was invented. The bounded scan verified no qualifying new evidence.

timeline.title: Consistency is not the same as stability.
timeline.type: Published-aggregate methods audit and regulatory notice
timeline.summary: Published force-matching averages change with the measurement window; high split-half consistency is not retest evidence. The scan found no new clinical result. A quality recall applies to one product batch.

timeline.title: A measurement needs its assumptions.
timeline.type: Primary-model audit and synthetic identification check
timeline.summary: A primary model and a synthetic example show why force matching needs a shared baseline before it can identify a mechanism. Older mixed-diagnosis evidence, a no-results protocol and an adjacent safety review remain distinct.

findings.title: Daily life belongs beside tic counts.
findings.summary: An adult qualitative study highlighted better treatments and practical daily-life priorities. A specialist-clinic sample cannot represent everyone.
findings.label: Isaacs and colleagues, 2024

findings.title: Persistence deserves its own attention.
findings.summary: A small blinded adult follow-up found observable tics in some people who reported being tic-free. Observation method changes what a study can claim.
findings.label: Pappert and colleagues, 2003
findings.linkState: Publisher HTTP 403; matching PubMed record verified via NCBI XML

findings.title: Shared improvement is not interchangeability.
findings.summary: Published treatment cohorts can show changes in both tic scores and quality of life. That alone does not show that one measure can replace the other.
findings.label: Ivanova and colleagues, 2026

activities.title: A hand at ease
activities.intro: Gently open and rest one hand in your usual supported position, if that feels comfortable.
activities.seated: Use your usual supported seated position. No stretching or stillness is required.
activities.standing: If standing is already comfortable, keep your usual support and let the hand rest naturally.
activities.rest: Imagine the movement, or rest. There is nothing to complete.

activities.title: A familiar little route
activities.intro: Consider a short stroll or wheel along a familiar level route, using your usual supports.
activities.seated: Stay seated and notice something familiar around you instead.
activities.standing: Choose only a route and movement that already feel comfortable for you.
activities.rest: Stay where you are, imagine the route, or skip it.

activities.title: Notice one comfortable thing
activities.intro: Notice one comfortable sound, shape, or texture nearby.
activities.seated: Look or listen from wherever you are comfortably seated.
activities.standing: If you are already comfortable standing, notice something nearby.
activities.rest: No need to pay close attention. Rest or skip freely.

activities.title: Familiar music, or silence
activities.intro: Choose familiar quiet music if you would enjoy it. Silence is an equal choice.
activities.seated: Listen in your usual comfortable position if you choose.
activities.standing: There is no need to move, dance, or keep a rhythm.
activities.rest: Choose silence, rest, or leave this idea for another day.

activities.title: A small mark or a silly sentence
activities.intro: Make a small mark, or say, type, or imagine a silly sentence.
activities.seated: Use a familiar comfortable way to draw, speak, or type.
activities.standing: If you prefer standing, keep your usual support. Imagining works too.
activities.rest: Do nothing, or imagine something amusing. Either is enough.

activities.title: Rest, or leave the page
activities.intro: Rest can be the whole idea. There is no progress to keep up with.
activities.seated: Settle into your usual comfortable seated position if you want.
activities.standing: Change to a usual comfortable position if that suits you.
activities.rest: Close the page or simply carry on with your day.
